column2: Your style.css is linked after Bootstrap's and contains this rule. What colour is the button while you hover over it? Code: .btn-primary { background-color: #ff5722; border-color: #ff5722; }

column3: Bootstrap's blue
Orange, the same as when you are not hovering
A slightly darker orange
See-through, because the rule removes the colour

column2: Bootstrap has a .btn:hover rule. That is a class plus a pseudo-class, which is more specific than your single-class .btn-primary, so it wins no matter which file came last. Its hover colour comes from var(--bs-btn-hover-bg), which is still blue. The fix is to set the variables instead: --bs-btn-bg, --bs-btn-hover-bg, and so on. See Example 01.
JavaScript and Java are two completely unrelated languages. So why is JavaScript called JavaScript?

column3: It was renamed in a 1995 marketing deal with Sun Microsystems, who owned Java
It is the version of Java that runs inside a web browser
Java and JavaScript were designed by the same team at Sun
JavaScript is converted into Java before the browser runs it

column2: The language was called Mocha, then LiveScript. In December 1995, Netscape and Sun announced a deal and LiveScript was renamed JavaScript, because Java was the most talked-about language of that year. That is the entire reason. Java is to JavaScript as ham is to hamster.

data-bs-toggle="#orderModal" on its own

A page is working correctly. You delete this line and reload: Code: <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.8/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.js"></script> What happens?

column3: The modal, the carousel and the navbar's menu button stop working; the grid, cards and colours are unaffected
The whole page loses its styling, because that file contains Bootstrap
Nothing: the data-bs- attributes do the work on their own
The browser shows an error in the Console explaining what is missing

column2: Bootstrap arrives in two separate downloads. The CSS file controls how things look; the script controls the things that move. Take the script away and everything visual is fine while every interactive component silently stops. And there is no error — nothing was loaded, so nothing complained. A button that does nothing, with an empty Console, is almost always a missing script.
Your button has data-bs-toggle="tooltip" and data-bs-title="...", Bootstrap's script is loaded, and the Console shows no errors. You hover over the button and no tooltip appears. Why?

column3: Tooltips are opt in: a line of JavaScript has to turn them on
Tooltips only work on links, not on buttons
You have to use the plain title attribute instead of data-bs-title
Tooltips come in a separate file that has to be linked as well

column2: Tooltips and popovers are the one exception to "the attributes are enough", and the reason is speed: a page could have hundreds of elements with a title, and setting all of them up on every page load would be wasteful. So you say which ones you want: Code: document.querySelectorAll('[data-bs-toggle="tooltip"]') .forEach(function (el) { new bootstrap.Tooltip(el); });

The button with id="orderButton" is clicked. What happens? Code: const toast = new bootstrap.Toast( document.getElementById("orderToast")); document.getElementById("orderButton") .addEventListener("click", function () { console.log("clicked"); });

column3: "clicked" appears in the Console, but the toast never appears
The toast appears
Nothing happens at all
The toast appears once and then stops working

column2: The first line gets the toast ready; it does not show it. A toast stays hidden until something calls toast.show(). The click listener is fine, so the Console message does appear. Adding toast.show(); inside the braces makes it work. "My code ran but nothing happened" and "my code never ran" are two different bugs, and console.log is how you tell them apart.
In Tailwind CSS, what does the class md:grid-cols-3 mean?

column3: Three columns, on screens 768px wide and wider
Three columns, but only on medium-sized screens
Three columns, on screens up to 768px wide
Three columns, each of medium width

column2: Like Bootstrap, Tailwind is written phones-first, so md: means @media (min-width: 768px). The rule applies from 768px upwards, including large screens, until a bigger prefix such as lg: overrides it. Below 768px there is no grid-cols at all, so the items stack in one column.
Which of these class attributes was written with Tailwind CSS rather than Bootstrap?

column3: class="bg-white rounded-lg shadow p-5"
class="card h-100 shadow-sm"
class="btn btn-primary"
class="alert alert-warning"

column2: Each Tailwind class does roughly one thing: a background, a border radius, a shadow, some padding. You build the look out of small pieces. card, btn and alert are Bootstrap's ready-made components, where one name gives you a whole designed thing.
Your opening-hours table is wider than a phone screen. You wrap it in <div class="table-responsive">. What does that do?

column3: Lets the table scroll sideways inside its own box
Shrinks the text until the table fits
Stacks the table's columns on top of each other
Hides the columns that do not fit

column2: The table-responsive div gets overflow-x: auto, so the table gets its own sideways scrollbar and the rest of the page stays still. Without it, a wide table makes the whole page scroll sideways — exactly the problem we spent Week 9 avoiding. We did this by hand in Week 7 with a table-wrap div; Bootstrap just has a class for it.

An element has class="card special". Both rules below use a single class, so they tie on specificity. What colour is its background? Code: /* bootstrap.min.css, linked FIRST */ .card { background-color: #fff; } /* your style.css, linked SECOND */ .special { background-color: #FFF8E1; }

column3: Cream (#FFF8E1): the rules tie, and yours is read last
White (#fff): .card is Bootstrap's own class, so Bootstrap wins
White (#fff): Bootstrap's file is larger and loads first
Neither: you need !important to override a framework

column2: The browser checks specificity first. Only when two rules tie does the order decide, and then the one read last wins — which is the whole reason your <link> to style.css goes after Bootstrap's. Compare this with Question 1, where the rules did not tie: there .btn:hover was more specific, and coming later did not help at all. Specificity first, then order.
